posts.note: New Year's Day essay on the creator economy, OnlyFans and Lilly Phillips versus ad-driven platforms and therapist platforms (Alma, Grow, Headway). Mostly present-tense economics and cultural critique. Four borderline forward-looking lines logged: two about creator earnings, one habitual 'will get screwed', one closing conditional 'someone is going to get F-d'. 'We have to pay for it' treated as advice and not logged.

Short explainer on the $2,000 Medicare Part D out-of-pocket cap that took effect at the start of 2025. Four statements: restatement of the cap, GLP-1 non-coverage becoming a 'hot topic', Lilly and Novo racing trials for coverage, and pressure on federal budgets and premiums.

Recap of an earlier newsletter publishing the authors' own 2020 survey (n=300) of clinician attitudes toward insurance. Results and methods are past; the Discussion, Solutions and Conclusions sections carry calls about insurance-based therapy platforms (Alma, Grow Therapy, Talkspace, BetterHelp), therapists quitting panels, and a shift to value-based or at-risk care. Several 'is essential' or 'must' sentences logged with normative flags for the coder to judge. One trivial personal commitment (no JAMA submission) logged.

statements.quote: Ms. Philips makes more money than you or I are ever likely to.
statements.context: OnlyFans creator Lilly Phillips reportedly earns tens of millions of dollars a year; the author claims neither he nor the reader is ever likely to earn as much.
statements.note: Borderline; a comparative claim about lifetime earnings rather than a dated forecast.

statements.quote: It won’t be a metric ton of money, on average. That is true across endeavors. Most people are not stars. The effort/star power ratio that is needed to support one’s family with fan-funded financials, however, is realistic for more people.
statements.context: After computing average OnlyFans creator revenue (about $1,177 ARR per creator) versus TikTok, YouTube and Instagram pay, the author states that fan-funded creation will not pay much on average but is a realistic way for more people to support a family than ad-driven platforms.
statements.note: Borderline; generic claim about average creator earnings, close to a truism. Compound claim.

statements.quote: Creators like Ms. Philips know they will get screwed, and by whom.
statements.context: Discussing OnlyFans' 20% take rate versus Substack's 10% and Alma/Grow's roughly 7%; the author says OnlyFans creators know they will be exploited by the platform, unlike therapists and doctors exploited by insurers and educational debt.
statements.note: Habitual 'will'; reads as a description of ongoing take-rate exploitation rather than a dated forecast.

statements.quote: But when we leave it to “others” to pay, far removed from our pocket books, personally? Someone is going to get F-d. It might even be… us .
statements.context: Closing argument: if society wants a world that values things other than sex and exploitation, people have to pay directly for newsletters, music or healthcare; when payment is left to advertisers or third parties, someone (possibly the reader) gets exploited.
statements.note: Conditional and generic; the preceding 'We have to pay for it' is advice and was not logged separately.

statements.quote: The best part of this law is that Medicare Beneficiaries will now be able to remember one number—$2000 a year, which is the most they will pay. That is of course unless they happen to require a medicine that isn’t covered under medicare part D.
statements.context: The $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap on Medicare Part D drug costs took effect at the start of 2025 (the post is dated 2025-01-02). The author restates the law's effect: beneficiaries will pay at most $2,000 a year for covered Part D drugs, with the caveat that drugs not covered under Part D are excluded.
statements.note: Restatement of enacted policy that has just taken effect; the law is referred to only as 'this law'.

statements.quote: That is likely to become a more “hot topic” (as I covered in this prior article ) because the following types of meds are not covered
statements.context: The exclusion of certain drug classes from Medicare Part D coverage (weight loss drugs, fertility drugs, cosmetic drugs, cold/cough, erectile dysfunction, vitamins, OTC), which the author says includes blockbuster GLP-1s, is expected to become a bigger public issue now that the $2,000 cap applies only to covered drugs.
statements.note: Author flags this as a restatement of a prior article.

statements.quote: Thus, the rush on the part of Lily and Novo to get all these remarkable trials done that prove their effectiveness in other indications— beyond weight loss—so that Medicare can cover them.
statements.context: Because Medicare Part D does not cover weight-loss drugs, the author describes Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk rushing to complete trials of GLP-1s in other indications so that Medicare can cover them.
statements.note: Borderline; describes a present strategy whose goal (trials completed, Medicare coverage) lies in the future. Medicare coverage is stated as the companies' aim, not the author's call.

statements.quote: This is good news for seniors and other individuals on Medicare, such as those with psychiatric or other disability, but it will put pressure on federal budgets and premiums.
statements.context: Closing assessment of the $2,000 Medicare Part D out-of-pocket cap: good for beneficiaries, including those with psychiatric disability, but it will put pressure on federal budgets and Part D premiums.

statements.quote: It does not mean that it will be submitted in some unbelievably stale format to JAMA Psychiatry, or any of the other journals that would give it prestige…
statements.context: The author explains that his and Carlene MacMillan's survey paper on clinician attitudes toward insurance is being published on the newsletter and will not be submitted to JAMA Psychiatry or other academic journals.
statements.confidence_phrase: does not mean that it will be
statements.note: Trivial personal commitment about the author's own paper and newsletter; the post is a recap of an earlier piece, so this restates the original.

statements.quote: The most important truth is that, for mental health conditions, a system that is stressful, feels controlling, and underpays you by a factor of many multiples of what you could be making otherwise is not a sustainable business model for clinicians.
statements.context: Discussion section of the survey write-up: the author argues the core problem with insurance for mental health clinicians is not workflow complexity but stress, control and underpayment, which he calls unsustainable as a business model for clinicians.
statements.note: Assessment with a forward implication (clinicians will keep leaving insurance); sets up the platform 'harsh awakening' call that follows.

statements.quote: Thus, the endless platform solutions that are doing clinicians a service by making it easier to take insurance are in for, possibly, a really harsh awakening unless they can change the way payers value the mental health clinicians in their network. Paying a few dollars more per claim is not going to cut it.
statements.context: Discussion section: insurance-enabling therapist platforms (the author names Alma, Grow Therapy, Talkspace and BetterHelp in the next paragraph) face a possible harsh awakening unless they change how payers value in-network mental health clinicians; small per-claim rate increases will not be enough.
statements.confidence_phrase: possibly; is not going to cut it
statements.note: Conditional compound claim: harsh awakening unless payer valuation changes; small rate bumps will not suffice.

statements.quote: This is a serious problem for the business models of all clinicians who take insurance and all mental health platforms. I’m looking at you Alma. I’m looking at you, Grow Therapy. This extends, of course, to Talk Space, Better Help, etc.
statements.context: Following the 'harsh awakening' warning, the author names the platforms whose business models he says are threatened by clinicians' rejection of insurance economics: Alma, Grow Therapy, Talkspace, BetterHelp and similar companies that create value off licensed therapists' work.
statements.note: Present-tense assessment that implies future trouble for the named platforms; borderline.

statements.quote: These force clinicians to take insurance as service platforms haven’t been around long enough to have their panels of therapists all quit.
statements.context: The author argues platforms that scale by having therapists take insurance (Alma, Grow Therapy, Talkspace, BetterHelp) are too young to have seen their therapist panels quit, implying that with time their therapists will quit, as 27% of surveyed clinicians had resigned from insurance panels.
statements.note: Implicit forecast: the sentence presupposes that platform therapist panels will eventually quit.

statements.quote: Maybe these platform solutions will do a better job of negotiating those contracts, but it’s not that much better.
statements.context: On insurance reimbursement rates for therapists (the author cites a $7 group therapy rate and under $100 to $200 per session for masters-level therapists versus $300 to $1,000 private-pay): platforms like Alma may negotiate somewhat better payer contracts, but not much better.
statements.note: Hedged; concedes a possible improvement and predicts it stays small.

statements.quote: A bunch of different companies scrambling to get pieces of that limited pie is going to make for a couple of exits, but it’s not gonna change healthcare.
statements.context: The author argues therapist time is a non-scalable, limited resource (45- or 60-minute blocks); companies competing for that pie (insurance-based therapy platforms) will produce a couple of exits but will not change healthcare.
statements.note: Compound: (a) a couple of exits; (b) no change to healthcare. Entities are those named earlier in the passage.

statements.quote: And therapists are going to quit. And then they’re going to go back to doing less scalable work, and everyone’s gonna be worse off.
statements.context: Continuation of the platform argument: therapists working on insurance-based platforms are going to quit, return to less scalable work, and everyone will be worse off.
statements.note: Compound claim; follows the 'couple of exits' sentence in the same paragraph.

statements.quote: And arbitrage on the difference between what we therapists think is nice and what people are actually worth is a fine strategy for a company until it’s not.
statements.context: Therapists offer sliding scales and reduced fees; the author says a company strategy built on arbitraging therapists' kindness against their market worth works only until it stops working.
statements.note: Implicit forecast that the arbitrage strategy of therapy platforms will stop working; borderline.

statements.quote: Training in fundamentals of payment systems could help clinicians navigate the insurance system. Still, this would not address frustrations related to bureaucratic friction and low reimbursement.
statements.context: Solutions discussion after noting 70% of respondents felt incapable of dealing with insurance: payment-systems training could help clinicians navigate insurance but would not fix bureaucratic friction or low reimbursement.
statements.note: Hypothetical conditional about an intervention; borderline.

statements.quote: Moreover, in order to win back mental health clinicians, insurance providers must offer solutions to address the poor reimbursement and administrative burden that drives clinicians into the private pay market.
statements.context: Solutions for Mental Health Clinicians section: insurers will not win back mental health clinicians unless they address poor reimbursement and administrative burden.
statements.note: Phrased as 'must'; predictive reading is conditional: without such solutions clinicians will not return to insurance. Coder may treat as normative.

statements.quote: Additionally, enforcement of existing laws that regulate mental health parity, prompt payment, and other statutes would make the adversarial attitude sometimes encountered by clinicians less “hazard free” for payers.
statements.context: Proposed systemic solution: enforcing existing mental health parity and prompt-payment laws would make payers' adversarial behavior toward clinicians carry consequences.
statements.note: Conditional on enforcement happening; no claim that enforcement will occur.

statements.quote: In a value-based model, outpatient clinicians would be rewarded for keeping their patients out of the hospital, thus directly linking clinician financial incentives with improved patient outcomes. In this shared risk model, clinician and payer goals would be more closely aligned and there would be less incentive for payers to block payments for needed care.
statements.context: Describing value-based care as an alternative to fee-for-service in mental health: under a value-based, shared-risk model, clinicians would be paid for keeping patients out of hospital, goals would align with payers, and payers would have less incentive to block payments.
statements.note: Conditional description of how a value-based model would behave; borderline between model description and forecast.

statements.quote: The opportunity for behavioral health providers who are willing to go “at risk“ and work in teams that approximate the acuity managed by IOP/PHP/some inpatient providers is coming.
statements.context: Solutions section: the author predicts that at-risk (shared-risk) payment opportunities are coming for behavioral health providers who work in teams handling IOP/PHP/inpatient-level acuity, and says providers need to be ready.
statements.note: Matches the at-risk outpatient model of the author's own companies (not named in the post); coder may consider CONTROL. Recap of an earlier piece.

statements.quote: We see a shift towards shared-risk, value-based care as a way to reduce the stress clinicians experience interacting with insurance providers.
statements.context: Closing of the Solutions section: the authors anticipate a shift toward shared-risk, value-based care in mental health that would reduce clinician stress with insurers.
statements.note: Stated as a perceived or anticipated trend; forward-looking reading is that value-based care will grow.

statements.quote: Correcting the misalignment of financial incentives in the traditional insurance model is essential for expanding the pool of clinicians willing to accept insurance and providing greater access to mental health care for our sickest patients.
statements.context: Solutions section: the pool of clinicians willing to accept insurance will not expand unless the financial incentives of the traditional insurance model are corrected.
statements.note: Normative 'is essential' framing with only a weak conditional predictive reading; logged for the coder to judge.

statements.quote: Continuing to study the experiences of mental health clinicians will further highlight these issues and lead to improvement in mental health care.
statements.context: Future Research section: continued study of clinician experiences with insurance will highlight these issues and lead to improvement in mental health care.
statements.note: Generic academic closing claim; borderline.

statements.quote: Value-based care would assist in reducing the contentious relations between mental health providers and insurance companies.
statements.context: Conclusions section of the survey write-up: value-based care would reduce the contentious relationship between mental health providers and insurers.
statements.note: Conditional on adoption of value-based care; restates the Solutions section claim.

statements.quote: Insurance is beneficial to mental health care, but increasing reimbursement rates, reducing fees, and providing better assistance are essential in order to continue to increase access to mental health care.
statements.context: Final sentence of the Conclusions: access to mental health care will not continue to increase unless insurers raise reimbursement, reduce fees and provide better assistance.
statements.note: Normative 'are essential' framing with only a weak conditional predictive reading; logged for the coder to judge.
